content.thinking: I'm compiling my findings: the abstract's adjusted result contradicts Table 5, several p-values in Tables 1 and 2 don't match the printed means and SDs, and the macronutrient percentages sum to about

findings.title: Abstract adjusted RMR beta -0.14 contradicts its own CI and Table 5
findings.description: The abstract and Results give the adjusted RMR association as beta = -0.14, 95% CI -7.05 to 19.25, P = 0.03. The CI is centred near 6.1 and spans zero, so it implies P of about 0.98, not 0.03. Table 5 (Model 2) prints 6.09 +/- 6.67 with the same CI and P = 0.362, so the abstract beta and P do not match the paper's own regression table.
findings.location: Abstract (Results paragraph); Results para 5; Table 5 RMR Model 2
findings.quote: Moreover, after controlling for covariates this association changed to non-significant (β = -0.14, 95% CI: -7.05, 19.25, P = 0.03).

anchors.quote: Moreover, after controlling for covariates this association changed to non-significant (β = -0.14, 95% CI: -7.05, 19.25, P = 0.03).

computed.table5_row_check: check_estimate_ci on 6.09 with the same CI recovers p 0.364 vs printed 0.362 (Wald); check_regression_batch at assumed df 268 reconciles 6.09/6.67 with p 0.362

consequence.explanation: The abstract's adjusted estimate is internally incoherent (non-significant label, P = 0.03, CI spanning 0); the Table 5 values (beta 6.09, P 0.362) reconcile with the CI, so the abstract/text beta and P look like transcription errors.

findings.notes: The tool notes its p recovery assumes a Wald interval; Table 5 shows the same CI is Wald-consistent with 6.09 and p 0.362, so the innocent reading is a transcription error in the abstract/Results text (beta and P), not a computation error in Table 5.

findings.title: RMR ANCOVA p reported as 0.041 in text, 0.05 in Table 3; trend 0.033 vs 0.03
findings.description: The abstract and Results state that adjusted RMR rises across LCDS tertiles at p = 0.041, with a trend p of 0.033. Table 3 prints P = 0.03 (unadjusted) and PAncova = 0.05 for RMR. A PAncova of 0.05 is not the 0.041 headline, and the significance claim sits at the alpha boundary. The 0.033 trend and 0.03 unadjusted values also look conflated.
findings.location: Abstract; Results para 3; Table 3 RMR row
findings.quote: There was a significant increase in RMR across tertiles and there was an incremental trend (p = 0.033) even after controlling for sex, age, occupation, education, smoking, physical activity and BMI. (p = 0.041).

anchors.quote: There was a significant increase in RMR across tertiles and there was an incremental trend (p = 0.033) even after controlling for sex, age, occupation, education, smoking, physical activity and BMI. (p = 0.041).

consequence.explanation: The abstract's headline significant adjusted RMR difference (p = 0.041) is not the PAncova printed in Table 3 (0.05).

findings.notes: No tool applies: SDs/ns per tertile are not printed (only CIs of adjusted means), so the ANCOVA p cannot be recomputed. Rounded 0.041 would print as 0.04, not 0.05. Also RMR is non-monotone (T2 1475 > T3 1438) while described as an increase across tertiles.

findings.title: Table 2 energy percentages of protein, fat and carbohydrate sum to about 102% in every tertile
findings.description: Mean percent of energy from protein, fat and carbohydrate is 13.6/23.2/65.2 (sum 102.0) in T1, 14.7/30.0/57.5 (102.2) in T2 and 17.2/36.0/48.8 (102.0) in T3. Macronutrient shares of energy should total 100% or less (alcohol), and means of per-person shares add to the same total. The excess of about 2 points exceeds the rounding window of 0.65.

consequence.explanation: The macronutrient composition used to define the LCDS tertiles does not add up, so at least one row is mis-stated or derived on a different basis.

findings.notes: Innocent explanation: percentages may be based on different denominators (e.g. energy excluding or including fibre/alcohol or FFQ-derived Atwater factors) or one of the rows is mistyped; the paper does not say. Per-item totals can exceed 100 only if energy is computed with factors differing from those in the percentage calculation.

findings.title: Table 1: p for BMI, visceral fat, RMR/FFM, waist is below anything the printed means/SDs allow
findings.description: For 4 of 10 continuous Table 1 rows the reported ANOVA p is smaller than the whole range reachable from the printed tertile means, SDs and ns: BMI 0.183 vs [0.335, 0.501]; visceral fat 0.094 vs [0.191, 0.331]; RMR/FFM 0.095 vs [0.179, 0.207]; waist circumference 0.477 vs [0.727, 0.795]. Age, weight, height, WHR, SBP and DBP are reachable. No row crosses 0.05.
findings.location: Table 1, BMI, Visceral fat level, RMR/FFM, Waist circumference rows

consequence.explanation: All affected rows are non-significant either way; the issue is reproducibility of the baseline p-values.

findings.notes: Tool default highly_suspicious, lowered: the paper says one-way ANOVA but non-normal variables (normality tested by K-S) may have been analysed with Kruskal-Wallis, and available-case ns may differ from the 92/78/98 header; neither is stated. Table 1 header n sums to 268, not 270, so n differs somewhere. 4 of 10 rows fail, checked in row order.

findings.title: Table 2: p for total energy, fibre, sugar unreachable from printed means/SDs
findings.description: For 3 of 22 Table 2 rows the reported ANOVA p lies outside the range reachable from the printed tertile means, SDs and ns: total energy 0.32 vs [0.438, 0.447]; fibre 0.80 vs [0.930, 0.983]; sugar 0.32 vs [0.411, 0.432]. The other 19 rows, including all 'p = 0.001' rows, are reachable. None of the affected rows is significant under either value.
findings.location: Table 2, Total calorie intake, Fiber, Sugar rows
findings.notes: Same caveats as Table 1: a non-parametric test, different available n, or covariate adjustment would explain it and the paper does not say. Rows reported as '0.001' were treated as the bound p<0.001 (the Results text states p<0.001 for protein/fat/carbohydrate).

findings.title: Table 1 RMR/FFM T3 SD of 31.4 is implausible beside T1/T2 SDs of 7.4 and 6.7
findings.description: For RMR/FFM the T3 mean is 31.3 and the SD is 31.4, while T1 and T2 have SDs of 7.37 and 6.69. An SD equal to the mean for a positive ratio, 4-5 times its neighbours, looks like a typo (e.g. 3.14). With SD 31.4 the reported p (0.095) is also outside the reachable range (see the Table 1 p-value finding).
findings.notes: Judgement from the printed row; no tool computes plausibility of an SD without a stated range.

findings.title: Text says linoleic acid did not differ across tertiles; Table 2 shows p = 0.001
findings.description: Results state that no significant difference was found in DHA, EPA and linoleic acid, but Table 2 gives linoleic acid P = 0.001 (10.3, 13.4, 18.3 g), and the same paragraph lists linoleic acid among the nutrients that were significantly higher. Linolenic acid (P = 0.07) was probably meant. The Discussion also names linolenic acid among nutrients higher in T3.
findings.location: Results para 2; Table 2 Linoleic acid and Linolenic acid rows
findings.quote: No significant statistical difference was found in mean DHA, EPA and linoleic acid.

anchors.quote: No significant statistical difference was found in mean DHA, EPA and linoleic acid.

findings.notes: rivets_anova confirms Table 2's linoleic p<0.001 is reachable from the printed means/SDs, so the table row is internally fine and the text is the likely slip.

findings.title: Discussion says LCDS predicts RMR after adjustment; adjusted regression is non-significant
findings.description: The Discussion states 'Greater adherence to LCDS was associated with higher RMR even after adjusting for confounding variables' and the Conclusion states a diet low in carbohydrates is associated with higher RMR. Table 5 Model 2 (adjusted regression) gives beta 6.09, 95% CI -7.05 to 19.25, P = 0.362, and the abstract itself says the association became non-significant. Only the tertile ANCOVA (p 0.041 text / 0.05 Table 3) and the crude r = 0.14 support the claim.
findings.location: Discussion para 1; Conclusion; Table 5 RMR Model 2
findings.quote: Greater adherence to LCDS was associated with higher RMR even after adjusting for confounding variables.

anchors.quote: Greater adherence to LCDS was associated with higher RMR even after adjusting for confounding variables.

consequence.explanation: The title/conclusion claim of an RMR association independent of covariates depends on the ANCOVA tertile contrast, not on the adjusted regression.

findings.notes: The two adjusted analyses use different covariate sets (ANCOVA: sex, age, occupation, education, smoking, PA, BMI; regression: age, sex, BMI, smoking, PA, energy intake), so they are not strictly contradictory; the Discussion does not say which it relies on. Authors also acknowledge the weak correlation and small sample.

findings.title: Table 5 crude R-squared for FM (0.05) and FFM (0.06) equal |r|, not r-squared
findings.description: For a single-predictor crude regression R-squared equals the square of the Pearson r. Table 4 gives r = -0.05 (FM) and 0.06 (FFM), whereas Table 5 Model 1 prints R-squared 0.05 and 0.06, the same numbers as |r|. The RMR row is consistent (r = 0.14, R-squared 0.02). The crude p-values (0.410, 0.320) match the correlation p-values, supporting that these are simple regressions.
findings.location: Table 5, FM and FFM Model 1, R² column; Table 4

computed.method: square of printed Pearson r from Table 4 (e.g. 0.05 squared = 0.0025); no registry tool covers R-squared vs r

findings.notes: Capped as a no-tool-exists comparison. Model 1 could include covariates (the paper calls it crude only in the Results text), in which case R-squared need not equal r-squared; but then the p-values would not match the correlation p-values so closely.

findings.title: Table 3 FFM T2: mean 49.4 sits far from the centre of its CI 41.5 to 52.2
findings.description: Every adjusted-mean CI in Table 3 is symmetric about its mean to rounding (e.g. 49.8 with 47.6-52.1; 51.1 with 48.3-53.9) except FFM T2, 49.4 (41.5-52.2), whose interval centre is 46.85. The lower bound is probably a typo (about 46.6). The tool returned consistent because no midpoint test applies to a plain mean without a stated scale.
findings.notes: Tool verdict consistent, quoted; I report the asymmetry as a reading flagged for the authors, not as a tool-backed problem. A skewed or bootstrap CI could be asymmetric, but the other 8 intervals in the table are symmetric.

findings.title: Table 1 sex percentages fit denominators 117 and 154, not the stated 115 men and 155 women
findings.description: The Male row (34.2, 27.4, 38.5) and Female row (34.4, 30.5, 35.1) are shares of each sex across tertiles. GRIM sweep finds joint denominators of 117 or 234 for males and 131/151/154/259/262 for females; the paper states 115 men and 155 women. The gap is 1-2 people (within ordinary missing data) and 117+154 would be 271, not 270. The Education 'Educated' row is only reachable at n = 197.
findings.location: Table 1, Male, Female and Educated rows
findings.notes: Rule 15: a gap of one to three people is ordinary available-case denominators; the paper does not state analysis denominators per row. Recorded as undecided, not as a defect. Sums of each row to ~100 were consistent.

findings.title: Three Pearson r values reproduce their printed p at n = 270
findings.description: r = 0.14 (p = 0.021), r = 0.06 (p = 0.323) and r = -0.05 (p = 0.412) in the Abstract, Results and Table 4 are consistent with n = 270; the printed p lies inside the range implied by the rounded r in each case (e.g. 0.14 gives p about 0.0214).
findings.quote: Also the variables LCDS and RMR (r = 0.14, p = 0.021) were found to be correlated weakly

anchors.quote: Also the variables LCDS and RMR (r = 0.14, p = 0.021) were found to be correlated weakly

findings.title: All six Table 5 coefficients reproduce their printed p from B/SE
findings.description: For the six LCDS coefficients in Table 5 (RMR, FM, FFM; Models 1 and 2), B/SE converts to the printed p within rounding, and the verdict is stable across assumed df of 10 to 100000. CIs are also centred on the estimates (RMR Model 1 18.81 with 2.55-35.07).
findings.notes: df is not printed; assumed 268 from N = 270, and tool df-sensitivity probes agree.

findings.title: Design sensitivity: N = 270 is below the 399 needed to detect r = 0.14 at 80% power
findings.description: For the headline correlation r = 0.14 the design (n = 270) falls short of the roughly 399 participants required for 80% power at alpha 0.05, and N = 270 has 80% power only for r of about 0.17. The authors acknowledge the small sample. This is context for a significant result near the boundary, not an error.
findings.quote: The correlation coefficient between RMR and LCDS is very low. It may be due to the small size of the sample.

anchors.quote: The correlation coefficient between RMR and LCDS is very low. It may be due to the small size of the sample.

findings.notes: The paper's own sample-size calculation (n = 256, E = 0.04) uses a proportion formula for 'older people' that does not fit a correlation/means design and does not state the assumed p; it cannot be reproduced.

findings.title: No duplicated mean/SD pairs within or across Tables 1 and 2
findings.description: Compared 60 mean/SD cells across Tables 1 and 2 (819 pairs): no identical pairs. One non-informative near-match (30.3 vs 33.0, a digit transposition) was returned and is not evidence.
findings.notes: Table 1 covers the same participants as Table 2, so the blocks are not independent samples; this is a within-table and coincidence screen only.

chi-squared p-values for categorical rows whose cell counts are not printed (percentages are row-wise shares across tertiles with unprinted denominators); recalc_chi_squared needs counts

unchecked.reason: Handoff to the proofreading agent: tertile ns 92 + 78 + 98 = 268, but the Methods report 270 analysed participants (check_summation_batch: difference -2). Participant-flow arithmetic belongs to the proofreading agent, so not filed as a finding here.

unchecked.location: Table 1 categorical rows (education, occupation, smoking, physical activity, overweight, obesity, family history)
unchecked.reason: Percentages are row-wise shares across tertiles with unprinted row denominators, so column n from the header does not apply and declare_table was not used; chi-squared p-values cannot be recomputed without counts. Only sex and education percentages were swept with grim_sweep.

unchecked.location: Table 3 ANCOVA p-values and adjusted-mean CIs
unchecked.reason: Per-group SDs are not printed (only CIs of adjusted means) and the covariate model is unstated, so F/p and effect sizes could not be recomputed; check_effect_plausibility was not run for the RMR tertile contrast for the same reason.

statcheck found 0 APA-format statistics (the paper prints p-values without df/test statistics); GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE not applicable: no integer-valued mean with SD, n and a printed range (the LCDS mean and SD are not reported).
The paper contains no figures; no figure captions or figure-only statistics to read, so the PDF cross-check was not needed (no table was alignment_uncertain or image_only).

multiplicity_report not run: 32 baseline/dietary descriptive comparisons are incidental, with no confirmatory claim depending on them; the primary RMR analyses (tertile ANCOVA, correlation, regression) are the claims that matter and are reported as nominal p near 0.02-0.05 without correction.

The calculated sample size of 256 (n = pq z^2/E^2 with E = 0.04, 'proportion of older people') does not state p and does not fit a correlation or means design; verify_power_analysis could not be run because the inputs are not stated.
